newsitem.title: GERMANY: German wheat price up, storeholders buy new crop.
newsitem.headline: German wheat price up, storeholders buy new crop.

text.p: German wheat prices have gained up to five marks a tonne over the last weeks on new crop demand from country merchants and storeholders, brokers said.
"Buyers believe German wheat will be able to compete with French on quality and with the British currency also firm they hope for price gains in the autumn," one said.
"Harvest delays have also underpinned the price."

The Hamburg grain exchange left its spot bread and feed wheat prices broadly unchanged for the fifth week running. 220 Hagberg/12.5 percent protein quality wheat was 265 marks a tonne and feed wheat was 262.50.
But German fob levels for new crop wheat were now starting at 272.50 for 12 percent Aug/Sept wheat in the 3,000 lot size, up 2.50, after large quantities of such "B" wheat traded for first half Sept.
A wide range of qualities, shipment sizes and dates up to December has become available since last week, with top prices for 10,000 tonnes Sept/Dec 14 percent wheat fob Rostock at 307.50.
Brokers also said flooding in the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Poland, which damaged crops and may raise food import demandr, helped lift prices.
In barley prices were seen unlikely to move unless the EU authorises more material for third country export, which means barley may be destined for intervention later this year.
Barley harvest progress was slowed by rain in the northern German export regions, with wheat still a few weeks off.
Yields are around 5.5-7.0 tonnes per hectare, weights 60-65 kilos per hectolitre and moisture is around 15 percent. National barley yields last year were 5.61 tph.

Ex-farm prices of 205-210 marks are 10-15 marks below those a year ago while wholesalers offer autumn barley at 230 marks. Nominal barley export prices for the new crop ranged between 235 and 252.50 marks depending on shipping date.
New crop rye was not in demand, with prices steady at 242.50-247.50 marks fob first half Sept.
